sense: say or show that something is true

terms.gloss: assure, state as certain; bear out
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; with an accusative, or an accusative and infinitive, and a dative of the person assured
evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.16.2: Balbus mihi cōnfirmāvit tē dīvitem futūrum
Cic. Att. 16.5.2: hoc cum mihi nōn modo cōnfirmāsset sed etiam persuāsisset
terms.comment: To tell someone for certain, or to prove a point with arguments (cōnfirmāre … deinde contrāria refūtāre, Cic. de Or. 2.80). Its first sense is to make firm or strengthen, and of people, to encourage (see encourage); Lewis & Short.

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; with an accusative, or an accusative and infinitive
evidence: Cic. Div. 2.8: nihil ut adfirmem, quaeram omnia
terms.comment: To state something firmly as one’s own claim, where cōnfirmō often assures someone else of it. Also written adfirmō.

terms.gloss: confirm by facts, make good; approve
evidence: Ter. And. 824: ut beneficium verbīs initum dūdum nunc rē comprobēs
terms.comment: To bear out by the event what was said; its commoner sense is to approve wholly of something (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Balbus mihi cōnfirmāvit tē dīvitem futūrum.
phrases.english: Balbus assured me you’ll be rich.

phrases.latin: hoc cum mihi nōn modo cōnfirmāsset sed etiam persuāsisset
phrases.english: when he had not only assured me of this but convinced me of it

phrases.latin: abs tē postulō atque ōrō Chreme ut beneficium verbīs initum dūdum nunc rē comprobēs
phrases.english: I ask and beg you, Chremes, to make good now in fact the favour you began in words a while ago

sources: Lewis & Short: confirmo · Lewis & Short: affirmo · Lewis & Short: comprobo
